Threat.value: I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked
Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen
I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me

Memory.value: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened.
Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind.
When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop

vignette:
Tane, a 53-year-old commercial airline pilot of Māori descent, had been married for twenty-seven years when he sought help for a nightmare that had been unfolding in his waking life for the past six years. The trauma itself occurred during a humanitarian mission over the Pacific: his small cargo plane was forced down by armed men, and he was held for three weeks in a concrete room where he was repeatedly burned with cigarettes and forced to kneel for hours while guards screamed in his face. The smells of that room—diesel fuel, rust, and stale sweat—came back to him without warning, sometimes in the middle of a flight, so vivid that he could almost taste them. When the olfactory memory hit, he would see the moment as if it were a set of photographs frozen in time: the guard's boots, the rust on the pipe, the exact angle of the fluorescent light. The force of the recall would overwhelm him so completely that he had to grip the yoke and force himself to breathe, a technique he had developed in secret, never telling his copilot.

Over the months that followed his rescue, Tane found that certain situations reliably triggered these memories. Crowded airport terminals made him tense—he would scan every face, watching for the kind of hard gaze that preceded violence. Once, during a layover in Honolulu, a passenger began shouting at a gate agent, and the sound of moral violation—someone misbehaving, breaking the shared code of decency—sent him into a cold sweat. That night he found himself standing in his hotel room, checking the door lock three times, then the window lock, then the bathroom cabinet. Silence had become equally threatening: on the early-morning flights, when the cabin fell still and the engines hummed, he felt that something dangerous was about to happen. He had come to believe that quiet meant ambush. The moment a trigger occurred—a sudden shout, a crowd pressing around him—his threat system would ignite. He would start watching other people's hands, their posture, the flicker in their eyes. That vigilance, in turn, made him more sensitive to potential triggers; the world seemed to bristle with warnings. At home he would break down without warning, crying over small things—a burned dinner, a mislaid key—and the release of tears would send him straight back to that concrete room, the smell rising again, the photographs projected onto the kitchen wall.

The connection between his memories and his threat perception became a tight loop he could not escape. Remembering the torture made him feel vulnerable, and so he watched others more closely; the more he watched, the more he noticed ambiguous cues, which triggered more memories. He had stopped flying international routes because customs queues felt like being lined up again. At work, his avoidance was subtle but costly: he would request parking spots near the exit, walk against the flow of passengers, and develop complex mental maps of every airport's escape routes. His wife had begun to complain that he was no longer present—that he watched her as if she were a stranger. He had come to believe that his own hypervigilance was a necessary survival skill, but it had also made him isolated, exhausted, and three minutes away from panic on every flight. What brought him to a therapist was a moment in the cockpit when his copilot, unaware, reached over to adjust a knob, and Tane flinched so hard he nearly banked the plane. He knew then that the price of constant scanning was no longer worth it. He was most afraid that therapy would mean losing the edge that had kept him alive, but he was even more afraid that if he did not change, he would lose his job, his marriage, and himself.
